The Use and the Abuse of Spiritual Gifts, Especially Prophesying and Tongues.<div eID="gen33632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33633" type="x-p"/> This is the second subject for correction in the Corinthian assemblies: the "first" was discussed (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.18-1Cor.11.34">1Co 11:18-34</reference>).<div eID="gen33633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33634" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17006"/><hi type="bold">1. spiritual gifts--</hi>the signs of the Spirit's continued efficacious presence in the Church, which is Christ's body, the complement of His incarnation, as the body is the complement of the head. By the love which pervades the whole, the gifts of the several members, forming reciprocal complements to each other, tend to the one object of perfecting the body of Christ. The ordinary and permanent gifts are comprehended together with the extraordinary, without distinction specified, as both alike flow from the divine indwelling Spirit of life. The extraordinary gifts, so far from making professors more peculiarly saints than in our day, did not always even prove that such persons were in a safe state at all (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.22">Mt 7:22</reference>). They were needed at first in the Church: (1) as a pledge to Christians themselves who had just passed over from Judaism or heathendom, that God was in the Church; (2) for the propagation of Christianity in the world; (3) for the edification of the Church. Now that we have the whole written New Testament (which they had not) and Christianity established as the result of the miracles, we need no further miracle to attest the truth. So the pillar of cloud which guided the Israelites was withdrawn when they were sufficiently assured of the Divine Presence, the manifestation of God's glory being thenceforward enclosed in the Most Holy Place [Archbishop Whately]. Paul sets forth in order: (1). The unity of the body (1Co 12:1-27). (2). The variety of its members and functions (1Co 12:27-30). (3). The grand principle for the right exercise of the gifts, namely, love (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.31">1Co 12:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.1-1Cor.13.4">1Co 13:1-13). (4</reference>) The comparison of the gifts with one another (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.1-1Cor.14.40">1Co 14:1-40</reference>).<div eID="gen33634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33635" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I would not have you ignorant--</hi>with all your boasts of "knowledge" at Corinth. If ignorant now, it will be your own fault, not mine (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.38">1Co 14:38</reference>). <div eID="gen33635" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 12 1Co 12:1-31 . The Use and the Abuse of Spiritual Gifts, Especially Prophesying and Tongues. This is the second subject for correction in the Corinthian assemblies: the "first" was discussed ( 1Co 11:18-34 ). 1. spiritual gifts-- the signs of the Spirit's continued efficacious presence in the Church, which is Christ's body, the complement of His incarnation, as the body is the complement of the head. By the love which pervades the whole, the gifts of the several members, forming reciprocal complements to each other, tend to the one object of perfecting the body of Christ. The ordinary and permanent gifts are comprehended together with the extraordinary, without distinction specified, as both alike flow from the divine indwelling Spirit of life. The extraordinary gifts, so far from making professors more peculiarly saints than in our day, did not always even prove that such persons were in a safe state at all ( Mt 7:22 ). They were needed at first in the Church: (1) as a pledge to Christians themselves who had just passed over from Judaism or heathendom, that God was in the Church; (2) for the propagation of Christianity in the world; (3) for the edification of the Church. Now that we have the whole written New Testament (which they had not) and Christianity established as the result of the miracles, we need no further miracle to attest the truth. So the pillar of cloud which guided the Israelites was withdrawn when they were sufficiently assured of the Divine Presence, the manifestation of God's glory being thenceforward enclosed in the Most Holy Place [Archbishop Whately]. Paul sets forth in order: (1). The unity of the body (1Co 12:1-27). (2). The variety of its members and functions (1Co 12:27-30). (3). The grand principle for the right exercise of the gifts, namely, love ( 1Co 12:31 ; 1Co 13:1-13). (4 ) The comparison of the gifts with one another ( 1Co 14:1-40 ). I would not have you ignorant-- with all your boasts of "knowledge" at Corinth. If ignorant now, it will be your own fault, not mine ( 1Co 14:38 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17013"/><div sID="gen33657" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17013"/>8-10. Three classes of gifts are distinguished by a distinct Greek word for "another" (a distinct class), marking the three several genera: allo marks the species, hetero the genera (compare Greek, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.39-1Cor.15.41">1Co 15:39-41</reference>). I. Gifts of intellect, namely, (1) wisdom; (2) knowledge. II. Gifts dependent on a special faith, namely, that of miracles (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.20">Mt 17:20</reference>): (1) healings; (2) workings of miracles; (3) prophecy of future events; (4) discerning of spirits, or the divinely given faculty of distinguishing between those really inspired, and those who pretended to inspiration. III. Gifts referring to the tongues: (1) diverse kinds of tongues; (2) interpretation of tongues. The catalogue in <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.28">1Co 12:28</reference> is not meant strictly to harmonize with the one here, though there are some particulars in which they correspond. The three genera are summarily referred to by single instances of each in <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.8">1Co 13:8</reference>. The first genus refers more to believers; the second, to unbelievers.<div eID="gen33657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33658" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by ... by ... by--</hi>The first in Greek is, "By means of," or "through the operation of"; the second is, "according to" the disposing of (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.11">1Co 12:11</reference>); the third is, "in," that is, under the influence of (so the Greek, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.43">Mt 22:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.2.27">Lu 2:27</reference>).<div eID="gen33658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33659" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">word of wisdom--</hi>the ready utterance of (for imparting to others, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.19">Ep 6:19</reference>) wisdom, namely, new revelations of the divine wisdom in redemption, as contrasted with human philosophy (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.24">1Co 1:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.7">2:6, 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.8">Ep 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.10">3:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.3">Col 2:3</reference>).<div eID="gen33659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33660" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">word of knowledge--</hi>ready utterance supernaturally imparted of truths ALREADY REVEALED (in this it is distinguished from "the word of wisdom," which related to NEW revelations). Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.6">1Co 14:6</reference>, where "revelation" (answering to "wisdom" here) is distinguished from "knowledge" [Henderson]. Wisdom or revelation belonged to the "prophets"; knowledge, to the "teachers." Wisdom penetrates deeper than knowledge. Knowledge relates to things that are to be done. Wisdom, to things eternal: hence, wisdom is not, like knowledge, said to "pass away" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.8">1Co 13:8</reference>), [Bengel]. <div eID="gen33660" type="x-p"/>

III. Gifts referring to the tongues: (1) diverse kinds of tongues; (2) interpretation of tongues. The catalogue in 1Co 12:28 is not meant strictly to harmonize with the one here, though there are some particulars in which they correspond. The three genera are summarily referred to by single instances of each in 1Co 13:8 . The first genus refers more to believers; the second, to unbelievers. by ... by ... by-- The first in Greek is, "By means of," or "through the operation of"; the second is, "according to" the disposing of (compare 1Co 12:11 ); the third is, "in," that is, under the influence of (so the Greek, Mt 22:43 ; Lu 2:27 ). word of wisdom-- the ready utterance of (for imparting to others, Ep 6:19 ) wisdom, namely, new revelations of the divine wisdom in redemption, as contrasted with human philosophy ( 1Co 1:24 ; 2:6, 7 ; Ep 1:8 ; 3:10 ; Col 2:3 ). word of knowledge-- ready utterance supernaturally imparted of truths ALREADY REVEALED (in this it is distinguished from "the word of wisdom," which related to NEW revelations). Compare 1Co 14:6 , where "revelation" (answering to "wisdom" here) is distinguished from "knowledge" [Henderson]. Wisdom or revelation belonged to the "prophets"; knowledge, to the "teachers." Wisdom penetrates deeper than knowledge. Knowledge relates to things that are to be done. Wisdom, to things eternal: hence, wisdom is not, like knowledge, said to "pass away" ( 1Co 13:8 ), [Bengel].

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17034"/><div sID="gen33705" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17034"/><hi type="bold">31. covet earnestly--</hi>Greek, "emulously desire." Not in the spirit of discontented "coveting." The Spirit "divides to every man severally as He will" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.1">1Co 12:1</reference>); but this does not prevent men earnestly seeking, by prayer and watchfulness, and cultivation of their faculties, the greatest gifts. Beza explains, "Hold in the highest estimation"; which accords with the distinction in his view (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.1">1Co 14:1</reference>) between "follow after charity--zealously esteem spiritual gifts"; also with (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.11">1Co 12:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.18">18</reference>) the sovereign will with which the Spirit distributes the gifts, precluding individuals from desiring gifts not vouchsafed to them. But see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.1">1Co 14:1</reference>.<div eID="gen33705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33706" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the best gifts--</hi>Most of the oldest manuscripts read, "the greatest gifts."<div eID="gen33706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33707" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and yet--</hi>Greek, "and moreover." Besides recommending your zealous desire for the greatest gifts, I am about to show you a something still more excellent (literally, "a way most way-like") to desire, "the way of love" (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.1">1Co 14:1</reference>). This love, or "charity," includes both "faith" and "hope" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.7">1Co 13:7</reference>), and bears the same fruits (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.1-1Cor.13.13">1Co 13:1-13</reference>) as the ordinary and permanent fruits of the Spirit (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.22-Gal.5.24">Ga 5:22-24</reference>). Thus "long-suffering," compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.4">1Co 12:4</reference>; "faith," <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.7">1Co 12:7</reference>; "joy," <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.6">1Co 12:6</reference>; "meekness," <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.5">1Co 12:5</reference>; "goodness," <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.5">1Co 12:5</reference>; "gentleness," <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.4">1Co 12:4</reference> (the Greek is the same for "is kind"). It is the work of the Holy Spirit, and consists in love to God, on account of God's love in Christ to us, and as a consequence, love to man, especially to the brethren in Christ (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.5">Ro 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.15.30">15:30</reference>). This is more to be desired than gifts (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.20">Lu 10:20</reference>). <chapter eID="1Cor.12"/>
entries.content_plain: 31. covet earnestly-- Greek, "emulously desire." Not in the spirit of discontented "coveting." The Spirit "divides to every man severally as He will" ( 1Co 12:1 ); but this does not prevent men earnestly seeking, by prayer and watchfulness, and cultivation of their faculties, the greatest gifts. Beza explains, "Hold in the highest estimation"; which accords with the distinction in his view ( 1Co 14:1 ) between "follow after charity--zealously esteem spiritual gifts"; also with ( 1Co 12:11 , 18 ) the sovereign will with which the Spirit distributes the gifts, precluding individuals from desiring gifts not vouchsafed to them. But see on 1Co 14:1 . the best gifts-- Most of the oldest manuscripts read, "the greatest gifts." and yet-- Greek, "and moreover." It is the work of the Holy Spirit, and consists in love to God, on account of God's love in Christ to us, and as a consequence, love to man, especially to the brethren in Christ ( Ro 5:5 ; 15:30 ). This is more to be desired than gifts ( Lu 10:20 ).
